modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are federal income tax withholdings?

modal-content.p: Your withholding is the amount of federal income tax withheld from your paycheck and other sources. If you’re an employee, your employer probably withholds income tax and pays it to the IRS in your name. Tax may also be withheld from certain other income — including pensions, bonuses, commissions, and gambling winnings.
If too little is withheld, you’ll generally owe tax when you file your tax return and may owe a penalty. If too much is withheld, you’ll generally be due a refund.
If you’re self-employed or don’t pay your taxes through withholding, you may need to pay estimated tax directly to the IRS as quarterly payments.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are estimated federal tax payments?

modal-content.p: Estimated federal tax payments are tax payments you made on income that can be taxed but isn’t subject to withholding. You may need to pay estimated tax if:

ol.li: You don’t pay your taxes through withholding, such as from a paycheck from an employer, or you don’t pay enough tax that way

modal-content.p: Estimated federal tax payments can be made:

ul.li: Through your IRS Online Account
Through options listed at irs.gov/payments (like paying online, by credit card, or by cash through a retail partner)
By mailing the payment with a Form 1040-ES
By phone
Through the IRS2Go mobile app

modal-content.p: Estimated tax payments are usually made on a quarterly basis in April, June, September, and January. Learn more about estimated taxes.

Are estimated tax payments listed on Form W-2?
No, estimated tax payments are different than what is listed on a Form W-2 in Box 2 - Federal income tax withheld. Don’t report as estimated taxes any amounts listed on a Form W-2. Those amounts should be reported in the Jobs section.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are overpayments from your federal tax return?

modal-content.p: An overpayment is when your total payments were more than the federal tax you owed.
When this happens, you can choose to:

ul.li: Take a refund
Apply all or part of your overpayment to the next year’s estimated federal taxes

modal-content.p: If you chose to apply your federal tax overpayment to your estimated federal taxes, you can find the amount on line 36 of your federal tax return.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: How should I handle joint tax payments I made with my former spouse?

modal-content.p: You can divide the amount paid in any way you choose as long as you both agree.

If you can’t agree, you must divide the federal tax payments in proportion to each spouse’s individual tax as shown on your separate returns for . When answering this question, enter your portion of the federal tax payment.
Follow the same guidance if you and your spouse filed your federal taxes jointly in and chose to apply an overpayment to this year’s estimated taxes.
For more information, refer to Publication 505, Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What if I made joint tax payments with my spouse who I’m filing separately from this year?

modal-content.p: If you and your spouse paid joint estimated federal tax but are now filing separate federal tax returns, you can divide the amount paid in any way you choose as long as you both agree.

If you can’t agree, you must divide the federal tax payments in proportion to each spouse’s individual tax as shown on your separate returns for . When answering this question, enter your portion of the federal tax payment.
Follow the same guidance if you and your spouse filed your federal taxes jointly in and chose to apply an overpayment to this year’s estimated taxes.
For more information, refer to Publication 505, Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What if I made separate tax payments from my spouse who I’m filing jointly with this year?

modal-content.p: If you or your spouse paid separate estimated federal tax, but you are now filing a joint federal tax return, add the amounts you each paid.

If you and your spouse filed your federal taxes separately in and chose to apply an overpayment to this year’s estimated taxes, include the total amount you contributed on your individual tax returns.
Follow these instructions even if your spouse died in or in before filing a federal return.
For more information, refer to Publication 505, Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax.
